\chapter{Which One, and the Form the Book Owed You}
\label{ch:ge-akkusativ}
\hlchaptermodality{47}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask which one and how many, put a der-word into the shape it takes when something is done to it, say that a thing exists, and leave an adjective alone when it follows the verb.}

Every der-word in the book is run through the shape it takes when something happens to it, and every adjective is run through the shape it takes when nothing does. The chapter costs five items and pays a debt the einen lesson wrote down in plain sight: GE-C14-einen told the reader to take einen 'as a word for now, not as a system', and named the chapter that would explain it. This is that chapter.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[welcher]{welcher — \textquotedblleft{}which,\textquotedblright{} and the two pieces inside it}

\label{lesson:GE-C34-welcher}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Wer} asks which person. \emph{Was} asks which thing. Neither can ask \textbf{which one of these}, and that is the word this lesson buys.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the three shapes of the negative article — \emph{kein}, \emph{keine}, \emph{keinen}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: welcher}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{welcher} — \textquotedblleft{}which\textquotedblright{}, standing in front of a noun.
\end{quote}

The ending copies the article the noun already takes, so you have nothing new to learn once you know its gender: \textbf{welcher} for a \emph{der}-word, \textbf{welche} for a \emph{die}-word, \textbf{welches} for a \emph{das}-word.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Welcher Hund?} · \textbf{Welche Katze?} · \textbf{Welches Brot?}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{VEL-cher}, with the soft ich-sound of \emph{ich} and \emph{nicht} in the middle.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{welcher} is two ancient pieces: \emph{\textbf{hwa-}} — the \emph{what} you already meet at the front of every W-word — and \emph{\textbf{-lîk}}, \textquotedblleft{}like, bodily form\textquotedblright{}, the ancestor of English \textbf{-ly} and of the word \textbf{like} itself. \emph{What-like.}

English built its own word out of the very same two: \emph{hwā} + \emph{līc} gave \textbf{hwilc}, which wore down to \textbf{which}. So both languages ask \textquotedblleft{}which one\textquotedblright{} by asking \textquotedblleft{}what kind\textquotedblright{}, and the shared seam is still visible if you set \emph{wel-cher} beside \emph{wh-ich}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say the article first, then the matching shape.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{der} Hund $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}Welcher Hund?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{die} Katze $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}Welche Katze?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{das} Brot $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}Welches Brot?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{der} Kaffee $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}Welcher Kaffee?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{die} Milch $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}Welche Milch?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Welcher Hund? Welche Katze? Welches Brot?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What decides the ending on \emph{welcher}? (\textbf{The article the noun takes.}) Give all three. (\emph{\textbf{Welcher, welche, welches}}.) What two pieces is it built from? (\textbf{Hwa-} and \textbf{-lîk} — \textquotedblleft{}what-like\textquotedblright{}.) Which English word was built the same way? (\emph{\textbf{Which}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wie viel · wie viele]{wie viel, wie viele — how much and how many}

\label{lesson:GE-C34-wie-viel}



\begin{quote}
You can count to twenty and you cannot ask anybody for a number. Say \textbf{zwölf} and \textbf{zwanzig}, then take the question that was missing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: wie viel · wie viele}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{wie viel} — \textquotedblleft{}how much\textquotedblright{}, for something you would not count. \textbf{wie viele} — \textquotedblleft{}how many\textquotedblright{}, for things you would.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wie viel Milch?} — how much milk. · \textbf{Wie viele Hunde?} — how many dogs.
\end{quote}

English draws the identical line with two words too, \emph{much} against \emph{many}, so nothing is new except the German for it. The \textbf{-e} on \emph{viele} is the plural ending you have carried since \emph{die}.

One phrase to bank whole: \textbf{Wie viel Uhr ist es?}, literally \emph{how much clock is it}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{viel} is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*pelh\textsubscript{1}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to fill\textquotedblright{}. Grimm's law turned that \textbf{p} into \textbf{f}, as it did in \emph{Fuß} against Latin \emph{pes}, and the word reached English as \textbf{full}. The same root sits in Greek \emph{poly-} and Latin \emph{plenus}. German asks \emph{how full} where English asks \emph{how much}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Decide countable or not before you speak.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item not countable — \textquotedblleft{}Wie viel Milch, Wasser, Kaffee?\textquotedblright{}
  \item countable — \textquotedblleft{}Wie viele Hunde? Wie viele Katzen?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the clock phrase, then the answer — \textquotedblleft{}Wie viel Uhr ist es?\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Es ist ein Uhr.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the \emph{p} that became \emph{f}, twice — \textquotedblleft{}Fuß und viel\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two questions side by side — \textquotedblleft{}Welcher Kaffee?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Wie viel Kaffee?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Wie viel Milch? Wie viele Hunde?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which one goes with milk, and why? (\emph{\textbf{Wie viel}} — milk is not counted.) Which goes with dogs? (\emph{\textbf{Wie viele}}.) What English word is \emph{viel}? (\emph{\textbf{Full}}, by the same \emph{p $\to$ f} step that gave \emph{Fuß}.) Ask the time. (\textbf{Wie viel Uhr ist es?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[den]{den — the form the book has owed you since einen}

\label{lesson:GE-C34-den}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{einen} and \textbf{keinen}. Both wear an \emph{-en} that no other shape of their word wears, and both were handed to you as plain words with the promise that the system behind them would come later. It comes now.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: den}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{den} — \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}, for a \emph{der}-word that is the thing being done to.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Der Hund} ist hier. $\to$ \textbf{Ich habe den Hund.}
\end{quote}

The dog standing is \emph{der Hund}; the dog being had is \emph{den Hund}. German writes the difference on the article rather than on the noun.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one row of three moves}]
\begin{quote}
When a noun is the thing being done to, only the \textbf{der}-words change shape.
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{naming it} & \textbf{doing something to it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{der} Hund & \textbf{den} Hund \\
\textbf{die} Milch & \textbf{die} Milch \\
\textbf{das} Brot & \textbf{das} Brot \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the whole announcement, and it is smaller than German's reputation suggests. \emph{Die} and \emph{das} stand still. So do their \emph{ein} and \emph{kein} partners — \textbf{eine}, \textbf{keine}, \textbf{ein}, \textbf{kein} — while \emph{ein} becomes \textbf{einen} and \emph{kein} becomes \textbf{keinen} on exactly the row where \emph{der} becomes \emph{den}.

Three words you already say, all moving together, all on one row. Nothing new has been added; a pattern has been pointed at.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
English ran this system too and threw nearly all of it away. Three survivors remain, all pronouns: \textbf{whom}, \textbf{him}, \textbf{them}. \emph{\textquotedblleft{}Whom did you see\textquotedblright{}} is precisely what \emph{den} does. English kept the marking only where it was shortest; German kept it on the article, where it stays visible on every noun.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Name it, then do something to it.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Hund\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe den Hund.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Wein\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe den Wein.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Kaffee\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe den Kaffee.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two that do not move — \textquotedblleft{}das Brot\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}das Wasser\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three that move together — \textquotedblleft{}den, einen, keinen\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask about it first — \textquotedblleft{}Wie viele Hunde?\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe den Hund\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}Wie viel Kaffee?\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe den Kaffee\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Der Hund — den Hund.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three articles changes when its noun is done to? (\textbf{Only \emph{der}, which becomes \emph{den}.}) Which two words you already say change on the same row? (\emph{\textbf{Einen}} and \emph{\textbf{keinen}}.) Which three English words are the last survivors of the same system? (\textbf{Whom, him, them}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Der Tag ist gut]{Der Tag ist gut — the adjective that stays still}

\label{lesson:GE-C34-praedikativ}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{gut}, then \textbf{guten Tag}, then \textbf{gute Nacht}. The same adjective wears three shapes, and you have never been told what decides which.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending comes from standing in front}]
\begin{quote}
A German adjective takes an ending only when it stands \textbf{in front of} its noun. After \emph{ist}, it stands bare.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Der Tag ist gut.} — bare. The adjective comes after the verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Guten Tag.} — an ending. The adjective comes before the noun.
\end{quote}

So the greeting and the verdict are the same word in two positions, and the position is the whole story. This is the single most economical thing in German adjectives: half of all the adjective forms in the language are \textbf{the dictionary word, unchanged}, and you get that half free.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
English does the opposite of both halves: it never inflects an adjective at all, in either position. \emph{The day is good}, \emph{good day} — one shape, always.

So every German adjective you own is already usable after \emph{ist} with no work:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Die Katze ist schwarz.} · \textbf{Der Wein ist rot.} · \textbf{Ich bin müde.}
\end{quote}

The colours from the colour chapters, the \emph{müde} from the wellbeing chapter and the \emph{gut} from page one all behave the same way the moment a verb stands in front of them.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item bare, after the verb — \textquotedblleft{}Der Tag ist gut.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with an ending, in front — \textquotedblleft{}Guten Tag.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the colours, all bare — \textquotedblleft{}Der Wein ist rot\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Die Katze ist schwarz\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Das Brot ist weiß\textquotedblright{}
  \item two more bare ones — \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Das ist schön\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two that emigrated to Romance — \textquotedblleft{}blau\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}blank\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Der Tag ist gut. Guten Tag.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When does a German adjective take an ending? (\textbf{Only in front of its noun.}) What shape does it wear after \emph{ist}? (\textbf{The dictionary shape, bare.}) Say the pair that has been on page one since the beginning. (\emph{\textbf{Der Tag ist gut\emph{ / }guten Tag}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[es gibt]{es gibt — \textquotedblleft{}it gives,\textquotedblright{} which is German for \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C34-es-gibt}



\begin{quote}
You met \textbf{es} as the weather's subject — the \emph{es} that stands for nobody. It has one more famous job, and it needs the form you learned two lessons ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: es gibt}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{es gibt} — \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}there are\textquotedblright{}. Literally: \emph{it gives}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Es gibt Kaffee.} — \textquotedblleft{}There is coffee.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Es gibt einen Hund.} — \textquotedblleft{}There is a dog.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Es gibt keinen Kaffee.} — \textquotedblleft{}There is no coffee.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The phrase never changes shape. Whether one thing exists or twenty, it stays \textbf{es gibt} — the \emph{es} is the same empty subject as in the weather, standing in a slot German insists on filling.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what follows it is an object}]
Because \emph{geben} means \emph{give}, the thing that exists is grammatically the thing being \textbf{given} — so it takes the done-to form this chapter has taught.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Es gibt den Hund.} · \textbf{Es gibt einen Hund.} · \textbf{Es gibt keinen Hund.}
\end{quote}

Every one of those is a \emph{der}-word wearing its \emph{-n}, and that is not a special rule for \emph{es gibt}. It is the ordinary rule, arriving in the commonest sentence you will ever want it in.

Four languages, four different verbs for the same idea: German \textbf{gives} it, French \textbf{has it there}, Spanish \textbf{has} it outright, English \textbf{puts} it there. Only German's choice makes the thing an object, and that is why \emph{es gibt} is the place a learner meets the case system whether or not anyone explained it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt Kaffee.\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt Tee.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the marked article — \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt einen Hund.\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt einen Wein.\textquotedblright{}
  \item negated — \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt keinen Kaffee.\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt keine Milch.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two uses of the empty \emph{es}, side by side — the weather, then existence
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt Brot und Wasser.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt keinen Kaffee.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{es gibt} say word for word? (\emph{\textbf{It gives}}.) Does it change when there are many things? (\textbf{No} — it never moves.) What form does the thing after it take? (\textbf{The done-to form} — \emph{einen}, \emph{keinen}, \emph{den}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}there is no coffee.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Es gibt keinen Kaffee.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Welchen? — the chapter, run cold}

\label{lesson:GE-R34-welchen}



\begin{quote}
Three questions first. Which row of the three articles moves? When does an adjective take an ending? What does \emph{es gibt} say word for word?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: which one, and how many}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three shapes — \textquotedblleft{}Welcher Hund? Welche Katze? Welches Brot?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the uncounted, then the counted — \textquotedblleft{}Wie viel Milch, Wasser, Kaffee?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Wie viele Hunde, Katzen?\textquotedblright{}; then \textquotedblleft{}Welcher Wein? Welcher Tee?\textquotedblright{}
  \item refuse each, choosing the negative — \textquotedblleft{}Es ist kein Wein\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}Das ist nicht gut\textquotedblright{}, and name the test
  \item as a command — \textquotedblleft{}Sieh den Hund!\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Hör den Hund!\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — every der-word, done to}
Every \emph{der}-word this book owns, moved. Name the article, then move it.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the drinks — \textquotedblleft{}der Kaffee, den Kaffee; der Tee, den Tee; der Wein, den Wein\textquotedblright{}
  \item the people — \textquotedblleft{}der Bruder, den Bruder; der Vater, den Vater; der Freund, den Freund\textquotedblright{}
  \item the body — \textquotedblleft{}der Arm, den Arm; der Finger, den Finger; der Fuß, den Fuß; der Mund, den Mund; der Kopf, den Kopf\textquotedblright{}
  \item the animal and the times of day — \textquotedblleft{}den Hund, den Tag, den Abend\textquotedblright{}
  \item three with \emph{es gibt} — \textquotedblleft{}Es gibt den Hund. Es gibt einen Bruder. Es gibt keinen Kaffee.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two bought far away against the two never lent — \emph{Kaffee} and \emph{Tee} against \emph{Fuß} and \emph{Mund}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: adjectives that stay still}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the colours after a verb, bare — \textquotedblleft{}Der Wein ist rot. Das Brot ist weiß. Die Katze ist schwarz.\textquotedblright{} Then \textquotedblleft{}grün, gelb, blau\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde. Das ist schön. Der Tag ist gut.\textquotedblright{} Then four verbs of the body, still yours — \textquotedblleft{}gehen, laufen, sitzen, stehen\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the three words that change together on the \emph{der} row. (\emph{\textbf{Den, einen, keinen}}.) Which two articles never move? (\emph{\textbf{Die}} and \emph{\textbf{das}}.) And what does \emph{es gibt} demand of what follows it? (\textbf{The done-to form.})
\end{tcolorbox}
